lesson.title: Protection: each fault leaves its own mark

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each fault's own mark, kW or kVAr flowing into a set or the fault current dying away, when you drag the time cursor through the fault you picked.
interactive.title: The fault timeline
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Fourteen small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Six show an idea, and eight ask you to try it. No marks, no timers.

The picture. Two sets, A and B, each 504 kW and 630 kVA, run side by side on one 440 V, 60 Hz board. Each set has a kW arrow and a kVAr arrow. An arrow points to the board while the set sends that power out. It turns round and is drawn red when that power flows into the set. Each set's breaker is drawn shut or open. Below, a panel changes with the fault. Engine stops: a timer bar that fills to the relay's delay. Field lost: a small drawing of A's E and V, with the load angle δ between them and a mark at 90°. Short circuit: the decrement curve of current against time, its three periods shaded and named, with a dashed line at the breaker's 2000 A setting, marked at 0.5 s. Overload: A's kW bar against a line at its 504 kW, and three 30 kW groups of non-essential loads that drop out in turn.

The controls. A Fault choice of four, in this order: Engine stops, Field lost, Short circuit, Overload, opening on Engine stops. A Time slider, the time cursor, opening at 0 s: 0 to 10 s in steps of 0.1 s for Engine stops, 0 to 2 s in steps of 0.05 s for Field lost, 0 to 1 s in steps of 0.01 s for Short circuit, and 0 to 15 s in steps of 0.5 s for Overload. An AVR supply switch, Shunt or PMG, shown only for Short circuit, opening on PMG. Four readout tiles, wrapping onto two rows on a phone, change with the fault. Engine stops: A in kW, B in kW, A in kVAr, Timer in s, the Timer hidden on screens 2 and 3 with its bar. Field lost: A in kW, A in kVAr, E in per unit, δ in °. Short circuit: Current in A, Times rated, and Above 2000 A in s. Overload: A in kW, Over rating in kW, Groups shed. The fault buttons wrap too, so no word splits.

The rule it computes. Engine stops: two sets share 400 kW at 0.8 power factor, 200 kW and 150 kVAr each. At 0 s A's engine stops. Its kW falls evenly over 1 s, a sketch, from 200 kW out to 50.4 kW in, 10% of its rating, an example figure. B carries the load plus A's draw, 400 − A's kW. The relay picks up once the inward flow passes 25.2 kW, 5% of A's rating, an example setting, at 0.9 s. Its timer fills over 5 s, an example delay. At 5.9 s A's breaker opens, and B carries 400 kW. Screen 3 asks with its own figures: two sets share 360 kW, 180 kW and 135 kVAr each, and A draws 40 kW, so B carries 400 kW. Field lost: the same 400 kW. V is 1.0 and Xs 1.5 per unit. A's E starts at 1.44, an example field, with δ at 19.3°. At 0 s the field is lost, and E falls by 0.8 each second, a sketch. A still sends out 200 kW, 200 ÷ 630 = 0.317 per unit, so sin δ = 0.32 × 1.5 ÷ E. A's kVAr = (E × cos δ − 1.0) ÷ 1.5 per unit, times 630 kVA. Below zero, it flows in. Once E falls below 0.48, near 1.2 s, no angle can carry the kW. The rotor slips: δ is drawn turning round, once a second, a sketch, and A's arrows swing back and forth. Short circuit: A runs alone, B shut down, and a fault strikes the board at 0 s. Rated current is 630 000 ÷ (√3 × 440) = 826.7 A. The sub-transient reactance is 0.15 and the transient reactance 0.25 per unit, example values, so 1 ÷ 0.15 = 6.67 and 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 times rated. The current, in times rated, is the sustained level + (4 − the sustained level) × e^(−t ÷ 0.3 s) + (6.67 − 4) × e^(−t ÷ 0.02 s), with example time constants. Screen 9 asks about a sub-transient reactance of 0.18 per unit instead: 1 ÷ 0.18 = 5.56 times rated. With a PMG, the sustained level is 3 times rated, an example: the AVR forces the field to hold it. Shunt-fed, it is 0, because the AVR's supply collapses with the output. The breaker opens once the current has stayed above 2000 A for 0.5 s, and its count restarts whenever the current falls below. Overload: two sets share 560 kW, 280 kW each. At 0 s B's breaker opens, and A carries all 560 kW. While A is over 504 kW, preferential trips shed one 30 kW group every 5 s, example settings. A ends on 500 kW, and the third group stays on.

Screen 1, try it, a recall. No picture. "A DC motor's armature turns in its field. What does it make as it turns?" Three choices, in this order: "A back-emf, pushing against the supply"; "Nothing, it only takes current"; "Extra current, helping the supply". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "Any coil turning in a field has a voltage made in it."; for the third: "Its voltage pushes against the supply, so it holds the current back." Why: "A motor and a generator are the same machine. Which way the power flows decides which it is." Read: the question.

Screen 2, show. Engine stops at 0 s, the Time slider free, the timer bar and the Timer tile hidden. The words: "Each fault leaves its own mark on a set's meters. Here two sets share 400 kW. Then A's engine stops. A's rotor is still locked in step with the board. So B drives it round as a motor. A's kW arrow turns round, and real power flows into A. That is reverse power. In this example, A draws 50.4 kW and B carries 450.4 kW. Drag the time cursor to watch it turn." Read: the words without the last sentence. Still: time 2 s, readouts A −50.4 kW, B 450.4 kW, A 150 kVAr.

Screen 3, try it, typed. Engine stops at 0 s, with its own figures: a 360 kW load and a 40 kW draw. The Timer tile is hidden, and the B tile reads ? until Check. "Now the two sets share 360 kW equally. A's engine stops. A draws 40 kW as a motor. How many kW does B carry now?" A field in kW. Answer 400 kW. Slips: 360, "B drives A round too. Add A's draw."; 320, "A's draw adds to B's load. It does not help it."; 220, "B carries the whole load, not just A's share." Hint when wrong: "B now feeds the load and A's draw." Why: "360 + 40 = 400 kW. That is still under B's 504 kW rating, so the board stays up." A right Check moves the time cursor to 2 s. Read: the question.

Screen 4, show. Engine stops, the timer bar shown, the Time slider free. The words: "A motoring set must come off. Its diesel can gather unburned fuel, a fire and explosion risk.[^1] And B carries A's draw, which can overload it. A reverse-power relay picks up once power flows in past its setting. Here that is 25.2 kW, 5% of A's rating. Then it waits, here for 5 s. Both are example settings. A brief reverse flow can come and go just after a set closes on. A stopped engine keeps drawing. So once the timer fills, A's breaker opens." Read: the words. Still: time 7 s, the timer full, A's breaker open, readouts A 0 kW, B 400 kW, Timer 5.0 s.

Screen 5, try it. The timer bar alone, its delay at 1 s. "The relay picks up at 25.2 kW and waits 1 s. Just after closing on, a set sends 30 kW back for 2 s. Its governor is still picking up load. The relay trips it. Which change stops this trip but still catches a stopped engine?" Three choices, in this order: "Raise the pickup to 60 kW"; "Lengthen the delay, past the 2 s"; "Switch the relay off while closing on". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "A stopped engine here draws only 50.4 kW. The relay would never see it."; for the third: "A set that stops just after closing on would go unseen." Why: "The delay sorts brief flows from lasting ones. A stopped engine draws for as long as it stays on the board. So a longer delay still catches it, and the pickup stays sensitive." A right Check shows a 5 s timer filling for 2 s and emptying. Read: the question.

Screen 6, show. Field lost at 0 s, the phasor panel large, the Time slider free. The words: "Now A's field is lost, and its E shrinks. Its engine still sends out 200 kW. Remember, power = E × V × sin δ ÷ Xs. So as E shrinks, δ must grow to carry the same kW. At E = 0.80, δ is 36.5°. A weak field cannot send kVAr out, so A draws 150 kVAr in. Once E is too small, even 90° cannot pass the 200 kW out. The engine still pushes it in, so the rotor speeds past the board's field. It slips a pole." Read: the words. Still: time 0.8 s, readouts A 200 kW, A −150 kVAr, E 0.80, δ 36.5°. Past the slip, the line under the picture says only that E is now too small for any angle to carry the 200 kW.

Screen 7, try it, typed. Field lost at 0 s, the phasor panel, the δ tile reading ? until Check. "A sends out 0.317 per unit of power. V is 1.0 and Xs is 1.5. Below what E does δ pass 90°, so that A slips a pole?" A field with no unit. Answer 0.48. Also accepted: 0.476. Slips: 0.21, "That divides by Xs. At 90°, sin δ is 1. So E × V ÷ Xs = the power."; 0.317, "That leaves out Xs."; 1.44, "That is A's E before the field was lost." Hint when wrong: "At 90°, sin δ = 1. So E × V ÷ Xs = the power." Why: "0.317 × 1.5 ÷ 1.0 = 0.48 per unit. A smaller E cannot carry 200 kW at any angle." A right Check moves the time cursor to 1.2 s, with δ at the 90° mark. Read: the question.

Screen 8, show. Short circuit on PMG at 0 s, the Time slider free, the supply switch hidden. The words: "A short circuit's current starts huge and falls with time. At first the rotor's windings hold on to their flux, and only a small reactance holds the current back. That grip fades through three periods: sub-transient, transient and sustained. This 630 kVA, 440 V set has a rated current of 826.7 A. Its transient reactance is 0.25 per unit, or 25%. As with a transformer, fault current = rated current × 100 ÷ the percentage impedance. So the transient period starts near 826.7 × 100 ÷ 25 = 3307 A." Read: the words. Still: time 0.05 s, readouts Current 3361 A, 4.07 times rated.

Screen 9, try it, typed. Short circuit on PMG at 0 s, with a sub-transient reactance of 0.18 per unit. The curve is hidden, and the Current and Times rated tiles read ? until Check. "Suppose this set's sub-transient reactance were 0.18 per unit. Its rated current is still 826.7 A. What would its first fault current be?" A field in A. Answer 4593 A. Also accepted: 4596. Slips: 148.8, "That multiplies by 0.18. Divide instead."; 3307, "That uses the transient reactance, 0.25."; 826.7, "That is the rated current. A fault draws many times more."; 5511, "That is the first current with 0.15. Divide by 0.18." Hint when wrong: "First fault current = rated current ÷ the sub-transient reactance." Why: "826.7 ÷ 0.18 = 4593 A. That is 5.56 times rated. It lasts only the first few cycles." A right Check shows the curve, with the readout 4593 A at 0 s. Read: the question.

Screen 10, show. Short circuit, the AVR supply switch and the Time slider free, opening on Shunt at 0.5 s. The words: "Now flip the AVR's supply. A shunt-fed AVR takes its power from the set's own output. A short circuit pulls that output down. So the field fails, and the current dies away.[^2] It falls below a breaker's 2000 A setting before its 0.5 s delay runs out. Fed by a PMG, the AVR forces the field. In this example the current settles at 3 times rated, 2480 A. The breaker trips." Read: "Now flip the AVR's supply." read as "Compare the two supplies at 0.5 s." Still: PMG, time 0.5 s, the shunt curve drawn faint beside it, readouts Current 2636 A, 3.19 times rated, above 2000 A for 0.5 s.

Screen 11, try it. Short circuit on Shunt at 0 s, the result hidden until Check. "A shunt-fed set feeds a fault. By 0.5 s its current is 625 A. A breaker downstream trips at 2000 A after 0.5 s. What happens?" Three choices, in this order: "The breaker trips at 0.5 s"; "The breaker never trips, as the current dies first"; "The AVR forces the current back to 3 times rated". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "By 0.5 s the current is well under 2000 A."; for the third: "A shunt-fed AVR's supply has collapsed with the output." Why: "The current falls below 2000 A near 0.15 s. So the breaker's timer never runs out. The fault is not cleared. Fed by a PMG, the set would still give 2636 A at 0.5 s." A right Check runs the cursor to 1 s on Shunt. Read: the question.

Screen 12, show. Overload at 0 s, the Time slider free. The words: "Last, overload. Two sets share 560 kW, and B trips out. A is left with all 560 kW. That is more than its 504 kW rating. Left like that, A's own overload protection would trip it. The board would go dark. So preferential trips shed non-essential loads first, in steps. Here each step drops a 30 kW group, 5 s apart. Two steps bring A to 500 kW, inside its rating." Read: the words. Still: time 12 s, readouts A 500 kW, Over rating 0 kW, Groups shed 2.

Screen 13, try it, typed (mixed). Overload at 0 s, the Groups shed tile reading ? until Check. "A 504 kW set is left carrying 590 kW. Each preferential trip sheds 30 kW. How many steps bring it within its rating?" A field in steps. Answer 3 steps. Slips: 2, "Two steps leave 530 kW, still over."; 2.87, "Steps come whole. Round up."; 86, "That is the kW over. Divide by 30 kW a step." Hint when wrong: "It is 86 kW over its rating." Why: "590 − 504 = 86 kW over. 86 ÷ 30 = 2.87, so it takes 3 steps. That leaves 500 kW." Read: the question.

Screen 14, try it (mixed). Field lost at 0.8 s, the readouts hidden until Check. "Set A's kW still flows out at 200 kW. But its kVAr arrow turns inwards, and its load angle climbs. Which protection should act?" Four choices, in this order: "Reverse power"; "Loss of field"; "Short-circuit overcurrent"; "Preferential trip". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "A's kW still flows out. Reverse power needs it flowing in."; for the third: "The current has not jumped to many times rated."; for the fourth: "Shedding load cannot bring back a lost field." Why: "kVAr flowing in while δ climbs is the mark of a lost field. Left on, the rotor slips a pole." A right Check shows: "Each fault, its own signature." Read: the question.
interactive.ignores: Time runs at very different speeds from fault to fault. A short circuit's first period is over in a few hundredths of a second. A reverse-power delay lasts seconds. The decays are smooth sketches with example reactances and time constants. The first fault current is drawn as the steady swing of the current. A real one can be offset on one phase and peak higher still. Each set holds its speed, so the frequency never sags. A real engine at full fuel slows on overload until load is shed. The lost field uses the steady rule for E, V and δ. A real machine slipping poles behaves partly like an induction machine. Its currents swing harder. The breaker has only a delayed setting. One with an instant trip set below the first current would open at once on either supply. Losses are left out.

explain.text:
A generator's protection works by spotting the mark each fault leaves on the set's meters. When a set runs in parallel, an engine that stops sends real power the wrong way. A lost field draws kVAr in and pushes the load angle towards 90°. A short circuit sends a huge current that falls with time. Each protection watches for one of these marks. First, the engine that stops. In parallel, A's rotor is locked in step with the board. So when its fuel goes, it cannot simply slow down. The other sets hold the board's speed and drive A round as a motor. Real power now flows into A. That flow is [[reverse power]]. Say two sets share 400 kW. As an example, A might draw 50.4 kW. B then carries 450.4 kW. Left on, a motored diesel risks fire and explosion from unburned fuel.[^1] B also carries A's draw on top of the load, so it can be overloaded. A reverse-power relay picks up once the inward flow passes its setting. Then it waits a few seconds before it opens the set's breaker. The wait sorts real faults from brief ones. A set that has just closed on can send a little power back for a second or two. That lasts until its governor picks up load. A stopped engine keeps drawing for as long as it stays on the board. So a longer delay cures a nuisance trip like this better than a higher pickup does. A higher pickup could miss a stopped engine that draws only a little.

A lost field shows a different mark. Recall that power = E × V × sin δ ÷ Xs, in per unit. The engine still sends out its kW. So as E shrinks, sin δ must grow to carry it. Take A carrying 200 kW on its 630 kVA rating. That is 200 ÷ 630 = 0.317 per unit. Xs is 1.5. With a healthy field, say E = 1.44, δ is 19.3°. At E = 0.80, δ has grown to 36.5°. The kVAr follows the part of E that lies in line with V. Once that part falls below V, the set stops sending kVAr out and draws it in instead. At E = 0.80, A draws 150 kVAr from the board. At 90°, sin δ is 1, its largest. So once E falls below 0.317 × 1.5 = 0.48, no angle can carry the kW. The engine still pushes the kW in, but the set can no longer pass it out. So the extra power speeds the rotor past the board's field. The rotor slips a pole and goes on slipping. The board then sees circulating currents and surges of torque and current. Loss-of-field protection watches for signs such as the inward kVAr. It trips the set, ideally before it slips.

A short circuit has a third mark. Its current starts huge and falls with time. Here is why it starts so high. The rotor's windings resist any sudden change in their flux. Any coil resists a sudden change in its current in the same way. So for the first few cycles, only a small reactance holds the current back. It is called the sub-transient reactance. That grip fades in two stages. The current falls through three periods, sub-transient, transient and sustained. Its plot against time is the set's [[decrement curve]]. Take a 630 kVA, 440 V set. Its rated current is 630 000 ÷ (√3 × 440) = 826.7 A. Say its sub-transient reactance is 0.15 per unit, an example value. The first current is then 826.7 ÷ 0.15 = 5511 A. Where it settles depends on the field. In the simple model, E behind Xs, a short at the terminals leaves only Xs to hold the current back. So the steady current is E ÷ Xs. Hold the field at its full-load E of 2.25. The steady current is then 2.25 ÷ 1.5 = 1.5 times rated, or 1240 A. To hold 3 times rated, the AVR must force the field to twice that.

That forcing needs a supply the fault cannot pull down. A shunt-fed AVR takes its power from the set's own output. A short circuit pulls that output down. So the field fails, and the current dies away to nothing.[^2] A PMG on the shaft keeps the AVR fed whatever the output does. So the set can hold its output while the protection downstream clears the fault. It is easy to assume every set holds a large fault current for as long as needed. Only a set whose AVR keeps its supply can. The last fault is overload. Sometimes one set is left carrying more than its rating. Then [[preferential tripping]] sheds non-essential loads in timed steps. The set and the essential loads stay on. Under- and over-voltage and frequency relays guard the board too. Each trips when its reading leaves a set band. These figures come from a simplified picture. It uses example settings and smooth decays, and its sets hold their speed. **Each generator fault has its own signature: power flowing in, kVAr flowing in as δ climbs, or a short-circuit current falling with time. Each protection is set to see its own.**

analogy.text: Think of the devices in a consumer unit. Each watches for one signature. An MCB watches the current against time. An RCD watches the difference between line and neutral. An RCD cannot see an overload at all. An MCB cannot see a small leak to earth. A set's protection works the same way. Reverse power, loss of field, overcurrent and preferential trips each watch for their own fault.
analogy.breaks: A final circuit is fed from the grid. Its fault current stays up until a device clears it, and your Zs checks rely on that. A set's fault current falls with time. A shunt-fed set's dies away. A final circuit also has no turning machine to drive backwards. So it has no reverse-power fault.

practice.text:
**When a generator trips**

The safe way first. Only people authorised to do it set and change protection, under your procedures. Do not raise a pickup or bypass a relay to stop a trip.

- Read which protection acted before you reset anything. Each one points to a different cause.
- Reverse power: look at the engine first, its fuel and its shutdowns. Did it trip just after closing on? Then close on with the incoming set running a little fast. It picks up load at once.
- Loss of field: look at the AVR, the exciter and the rotating diodes before the set runs again.
- Short circuit or overcurrent: find and clear the fault before the board is made live again.
- Preferential trip: put the shed loads back only once enough sets are on the board to carry them.
- Under- and over-voltage and under- and over-frequency protection each watch the board's own voltage or frequency against a band.

**Rules of thumb:** rated current = kVA ÷ (√3 × V). The first fault current is the rated current ÷ the sub-transient reactance. With its field held, a set's steady fault current is E ÷ Xs times rated. A shunt-fed set's fault current dies away. A set whose AVR is fed by a PMG can hold it.

**Worked example:** Will a set's fault current trip a breaker? The set is 630 kVA at 440 V. Its rated current is 630 000 ÷ (√3 × 440) = 826.7 A. Its sub-transient reactance is 0.15. So the first current is 826.7 ÷ 0.15 = 5511 A. A breaker downstream trips at 2000 A after 0.5 s. On the example curve, a shunt-fed set's current has fallen to 625 A by 0.5 s. So the breaker never trips. Now feed its AVR from a PMG. On the example curve, the current at 0.5 s is still 2636 A. It settles later at 3 × 826.7 = 2480 A. Both are over 2000 A, so the breaker trips at 0.5 s. So check each breaker against the set's current at the breaker's own trip time. Read that current off the decrement curve. Do not check only against the first current.

**Common mistakes**
- Raising the reverse-power pickup to stop nuisance trips. A longer delay is the better cure. It still catches a stopped engine.
- Assuming every set holds 3 times its rated current in a fault. A shunt-fed set's current dies away.
- Judging discrimination on the first fault current alone. What counts is the current at each device's trip time.
- Reading a lost field as an overload. The kW stays put while the kVAr turns inwards.

checks.label: Engine stops: A falls from 200 kW out to 50.4 kW in over 1 s; the relay picks up at 25.2 kW in, at 0.9 s, and A's breaker opens 5 s later, at 5.9 s
Screen 2 at 2 s: A reads −50.4 kW with its kW arrow red into A, B 450.4 kW, A 150 kVAr; screen 3, sharing 360 kW with A drawing 40 kW, shows ? for B until checked, then 400 at 2 s
Screen 4 at 7 s: the timer full at 5.0 s, A's breaker open, A 0 kW and B 400 kW
Screen 5: a 1 s delay fills during the 2 s flow and trips; a 5 s delay reaches 2 s, then resets with no trip
Field lost: E 1.44 carries 200 kW at δ 19.3°; at 0.8 s E is 0.80, δ 36.5°, and A draws 150 kVAr while its kW still flows out
0.317 × 1.5 ÷ 1.0 = 0.48: below it δ passes 90°, near 1.2 s; screen 7 shows ? for δ until checked, then E 0.48 and δ 90.0
A loss of excitation in parallel brings pole slipping and oscillation: past 90°, δ keeps turning and A's kW swings out and in
Rated current 630 000 ÷ (√3 × 440) = 826.7 A; the first current 826.7 ÷ 0.15 = 5511 A, 6.67 times; at 0.05 s screen 8 reads 3361 A, 4.07 times
Screen 9, with 0.18, hides the curve and shows ? for the current until checked, then 4593 A, 5.56 times rated, at 0 s
Screen 10 at 0.5 s: with a PMG 2636 A, 3.19 times rated, above 2000 A for 0.50 s, and the breaker trips; shunt-fed, 625 A and no trip
Screen 11 hides the curves and readouts until checked; once checked the shunt-fed current has died to 118 A at 1 s and the breaker never tripped
Self-excited alternators do not maintain a short-circuit current: shunt-fed, it decays towards 0, under 2000 A near 0.15 s and 625 A by 0.5 s
With a PMG the set sustains its output during a short circuit, so the protection has time to clear the fault: it holds 2480 A, and the breaker trips at 0.5 s
The fault current runs through sub-transient, transient and sustained periods: from 6.67 times rated it loses its sub-transient part within 0.1 s, then settles on its sustained level
Real power flows into the generator when it loses its prime-mover input, and the relay detects it: from 1 s on A draws power, and the relay picks up only once 25.2 kW flows in

Overload: B trips out and A carries 560 kW, 56 over; a 30 kW group goes every 5 s, so at 12 s A carries 500 kW with two groups shed and the third on; from 590 kW three steps bring it to 500 kW at 15 s
Screen 14 hides the readouts and the cause until checked, while A's kW arrow points out and its kVAr arrow in; once checked, it names the field lost
Holding the full-load E of 2.25 gives 2.25 ÷ 1.5 = 1.5 times rated, 1240 A; holding 3 times rated needs twice that field
Fourteen screens, six that show and eight to try

applied.problem: Three claims are wider than true: an engine stopping only reverses power on a set in parallel; a longer delay is the better cure, not the only one (closing on a little fast also cures it); loss-of-field relays do not always trip before the rotor slips.

"Not against the first current" is too absolute: a breaker with an instantaneous element trips on the first current, so it must be checked too; and the longer delay is the better cure for nuisance trips, not the only one, since the practice itself also says close on a little fast.
Screen 10 states the PMG sustained level of 3 times rated as fact, but it is an assumed example value; the number rule needs it worded as chosen.
